newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Aid appeal to be launched for Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Aid appeal to be launched for Afghanistan.

text.p: The international community is to launch on Tuesday a consolidated appeal for funds to aid wartorn Afghanistan under the coordination of the United Nations.
"The focus of the appeal is to meet the urgent humanitarian and rehabilitation needs of Afghanistan," a U.N. source said.

Most of Afghanistan's social and civil structures have been destroyed or badly damaged by 17 years of war. The United Nations estimates that there are 10 million landmines and that as many as 10 people are injured each day.

More than two million Afghans live as refugees outside the country, and many others have been internally displaced by the four years of factional fighting that have riven the country since the fall of the communist government in 1992.
Afghanistan has one of the lowest life expectancies and highest infant mortality rates in the world. One in four Afghan children die before their fifth birthday.
Previous appeals by the international community for funds to alleviate the suffering in Afghanistan have met with disappointing results.
In 1996, the United Nations and non-governmental agencies (NGOs) in Afghanistan appealed for $124 million. They received $56 million.

Observers say that the length of the conflict in Afghanistan and the lack of any prospect of peace have discouraged donors from contributing to the appeal. They also say that the conflicts in Somalia and Rwanda have taken funds that might otherwise have been sent to Afghanistan.

Even before the launch of the appeal, some NGOs have expressed concern that the policies of the Islamic Taleban, particularly their treatment of women, would make it even more difficult to raise funds from donor nations.
Under their rule, the Taleban have closed girl's schools and denied most women the right to work in the parts of Afghanistan they control.
The Taleban took control of the capital Kabul in late September, giving the purist Islamic group control of more than two thirds of the country.
The group are fighting the forces of the ousted government and a northern warlord on two fronts, one just north of Kabul and another in the northwest of the country.
Most of the aid work in Afghanistan is aimed at emergency relief, and the provision of basic services such as water and sanitation.
The United Nations estimated that almost half of the population of Kabul -- about 600,000 people -- receive some of their food, as well as other forms of aid, from international organisations.
Aid officials say that much of the long-term rehabilitation that the country needs will have to wait until peace comes.
